name: Elena Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Elena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm a junior buyer at a food-service distributor that supplies about three hundred restaurants and cafés, and I handle dry goods: flour, rice, cooking oil, tinned tomatoes. I'm in by eight, check what the warehouse sold overnight, then spend most of the morning on the phone and email with suppliers chasing prices and delivery dates. Afternoons I build the purchase orders and get them signed off by Priya, the senior buyer who's been teaching me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the deal part, when a supplier rings back and I've knocked twenty cents off a case of oil. What wears me out is the spreadsheets, honestly, I'm still slow at them and I make mistakes Priya has to catch. I've been there eighteen months and some days I still feel like the new girl.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about home.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Tomás, he drives a city bus, and we rent a two-bedroom flat above a laundrette. We've got about three months of bills saved, which feels okay until the rent goes up again. No kids yet, maybe in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say I told you so, to be honest. Half the trade magazines have been saying AI will run purchasing, and if it doesn't, I'd post something like, good, people still matter. At work I'd just say it's a nice tool for drafting emails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved, but I'm not sure my job is that safe anyway. Our margins are tiny and the owners keep talking about cutting costs. The routine bits AI does take, like matching invoices, are exactly the bits a junior like me does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and try to get faster at the spreadsheets so Priya stops fixing my work. I'd ask about a short evening course in purchasing that the trade association runs, maybe two hundred for the term. And I'd keep putting a bit into savings each month because the rent keeps creeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, but with a little knot in my stomach. The AI part isn't the worry, it's whether the company holds up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the invoice matching is the part a junior does. How much of your week is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a day a week, Fridays mostly. If software took that, I'd have to show I'm worth keeping for the phone work, and I'm not the best negotiator in the office yet. Priya is, by a mile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomás if the owners announced cuts, even in this quieter picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we hold off on the bigger flat and keep the three months saved. Even in a world where AI is all hype, a junior buyer at a cheap distributor is first in line when the owners cut costs.

say: I'd say AI turned out to be a **drafting tool**, not a replacement for buyers.
I'd post that **people still matter** in purchasing, because supplier relationships are built on the phone.
think: The **invoice matching** AI does take is exactly the routine work a junior like me does on Fridays.
The bigger risk is the **owners cutting costs** at a low-margin distributor, AI or no AI.
do: Get **faster at spreadsheets** so Priya stops correcting my purchase orders.
Sign up for the trade association's **evening purchasing course**, about two hundred for the term.
Keep adding to the **three months of savings** while the rent creeps up.
feel: Mostly **steady**, with a small **knot** about whether the company holds up.
S0.quote: Even in a world where AI is all hype, a junior buyer at a cheap distributor is first in line when the owners cut costs.
fieldNote: Her worry in AI Plateau is the **thin-margin employer**, not the technology itself.
She sees **invoice matching** as her own routine work, so even a small AI change touches her.
She admires Priya (the senior buyer) and measures herself against her **negotiating skill**.

steps.text: Keep building dry-goods purchase orders and chase supplier prices by phone
Take the trade association's evening purchasing course this term
Hold three months of rent and bills in savings before moving flats

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need to get ahead of it together, not each person for themselves. Online I'd probably share stuff about unions pushing for retraining money. I'd say the companies saving millions should pay for people to learn the new systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job as it is now goes. Buying flour and oil from the same twenty suppliers on a set schedule is exactly what a computer can plan. Priya might stay to handle the big contracts, but juniors like me are the bit they'd trim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until a couple of people in the office had tried the new ordering software, then learn it properly, not just poke at it. I'd talk to the shop steward at the warehouse about whether office staff can join the union. And I'd start looking at supplier-side jobs, like account manager for a mill, where you still visit restaurants in person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. It's not the end of the world, but it's my first real job and I'd only just started to feel good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a normal Tuesday look like in that world, if you were still there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be checking what the system ordered instead of ordering it myself. That's a job for one person, not three. Fewer calls, more staring at a screen asking why it picked the expensive rice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Danny in accounts payable, he's fifty-eight and he still prints out every invoice. If the matching goes automatic, he's gone, and nobody's going to hire him somewhere else. I'd want the union talking about him, not just about people like me.

say: I'd say we need to **adapt together**, with companies funding the retraining for staff.
I'd share posts about **unions pushing** for retraining money from firms that save millions.
think: My job ordering **dry goods** on a set schedule is exactly what software can plan.
Priya keeps the big contracts, but **juniors get trimmed** when three buyers become one.
do: Learn the **new ordering software** properly once two colleagues have tried it.
Ask the warehouse **shop steward** whether office staff can join the union.
Look at **supplier-side account manager** jobs that still involve visiting restaurants.
feel: **Anxious**, because it's her first real job and she'd only just felt good at it.
Protective of older colleagues like Danny who have **fewer options**.
S1.quote: I think I'd be checking what the system ordered instead of ordering it myself. That's a job for one person, not three.
fieldNote: She expects her **own role** to be cut, not just changed, which puts her at anxious.
Her **union instinct** extends to colleagues, especially Danny (accounts payable, 58).
She waits for proof before learning tools, which fits her **steady** adaptability.

steps.text: Learn the new ordering software once two colleagues have tried it
Ask the warehouse shop steward about office staff joining the union
Apply for account manager jobs at flour mills and oil suppliers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going way too fast and the government needs to step in now, not after half of us are out of work. I'd be the one sharing every petition about a pause or a jobs guarantee. At work I'd say it straight: none of us were ready for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm out of a job by the end of 2028. My whole day is thinking work at a desk: prices, orders, emails. The warehouse lads get until about 2031 because the robots come later, but that's three years, not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now, before it arrives, I'd move half our savings into an account we don't touch and stop eating out on Fridays. I'd go talk to the warehouse manager about switching to the floor, picking or driving a forklift, because hands-on work has those extra years. And I'd join whatever union or campaign is pushing for income support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. It's like knowing the bus is coming and you can't get off the road fast enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd move to the warehouse floor. How would that feel, going from buyer to picker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit humiliating, if I'm honest, because I worked hard to get off the floor in my first job at a supermarket. But a pay cheque is a pay cheque. And it buys me about three years to figure out the next thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Tomás cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday to his parents' place, that's eight hundred we'd keep instead. Then the gym and the streaming stuff. Tomás drives a bus, so his job lasts until the robots come too, and that's what we'd be living on.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and the government must step in before people lose work.
I'd share **petitions** for a pause or a **jobs guarantee** and say none of us were ready.
think: My job is all **desk thinking work**, so I expect to lose it by the end of **2028**.
Warehouse and driving work get about **three extra years**, which is breathing room, not safety.
do: Move half the savings into a **locked account** and stop eating out on Fridays.
Ask the warehouse manager about switching to **picking or forklift work** before 2028.
Join the **union campaign** pushing for income support for displaced workers.
feel: **Scared**, like watching a bus coming and not getting off the road in time.
A bit **humiliated** at the idea of going back to warehouse work.
S2.quote: My whole day is thinking work at a desk: prices, orders, emails. The warehouse lads get until about 2031 because the robots come later, but that's three years, not forever.
fieldNote: She clearly separates her **desk work** from the warehouse's **hands-on work** and their different dates.
The household would lean on Tomás (her partner, bus driver), whose job lasts until the **robots arrive**.
Stepping back to the floor stings her **pride**, but she'd do it for the pay cheque.

steps.text: Move half the savings into a separate account and leave it alone
Skip the eight-hundred trip to Tomás's parents and cancel the gym
Ask the warehouse manager for a picking or forklift job
Join the union campaign for income support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them, and I'd mean the government and the companies, not just workers. I'd probably go to a couple of meetings about it. People listen more when it's not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still think the buyer job is gone, just around 2031 instead of 2028. The difference is I'd have time to get a forklift licence, maybe a heavy goods licence, and I'd be thirty-two, not twenty-nine. Hands-on work lasts until around 2034, so that's real time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the forklift licence at the warehouse's training day, it's free for staff. I'd start the heavy goods driving course next year, about two thousand, which I'd save for. And I'd keep using the AI tools at work now and then so I'm not lost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but less frantic. It's still a cliff, but I can see the edge from a distance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why driving, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomás says the bus depot is always short of drivers. And it's a job where you're actually doing something with your hands, so the robots come later. I'd rather be ahead of the queue than in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said the buyer job goes. Do you still think you'd be anxious in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because it's still my income that goes, just slower. I'd have a plan, though, which makes me feel less sick about it. A five-year warning gives me time to get a heavy goods driving licence before everyone else in the office wants one.

say: I'd say we have **five years**, so governments and companies must use them, not just workers.
I'd go to **public meetings**, because people listen more when it isn't panic.
think: The **buyer job** still goes, around **2031** instead of 2028.
Hands-on driving work lasts until about **2034**, giving me real time to switch.
do: Take the free **forklift licence** at the warehouse's staff training day this year.
Save about **two thousand** for a heavy goods driving course next year.
Keep using **AI tools** at work now and then so the new systems aren't foreign.
feel: Still **uneasy**, but less frantic because she can see the **edge** coming.
S3.quote: A five-year warning gives me time to get a heavy goods driving licence before everyone else in the office wants one.
fieldNote: The **extra three years** turn her plan from scramble to a sequence of licences.
She still expects to **lose her income** from buying, so anxious rather than uneasy.
Tomás (her partner) and his bus depot shape her **driving plan**.

steps.text: Take the free forklift licence at the warehouse training day
Save two thousand for a heavy goods driving course
Use the AI ordering tools now and then at work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, if the government actually plans. I'd push for free retraining and a shorter working week, like the unions talk about. At work I'd say let's not waste the warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think it's the same end, but I'd be thirty-seven by 2036, with maybe a kid. That's a different person losing a job. The robots come around 2039, so even the hands-on fallback runs out about when I'd be forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in buying for a few years and get properly good at it, because the job's still there. I'd do a part-time course in logistics or something like that over three years. And Tomás and I would think hard about whether to buy a flat or keep renting, because a mortgage with no job is a nightmare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in a slow way. It's a long fuse, but it's still lit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change when you have children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably we'd have them sooner, actually, while we both still have jobs and the maternity pay is real. That sounds strange, but I'd rather have a baby at thirty with a job than at thirty-six without one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the one thing you'd want from your employer in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tell us early. If the owners know they're buying a system in 2034, say so in 2030. Priya would tell me, I trust her, but the owners never tell anyone anything until the redundancy letters come.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough to plan, if the government actually does it.
I'd push for **free retraining** and a **shorter week**, as the unions propose.
think: I'd be **thirty-seven** by 2036, possibly with a child, which is a harder time to lose work.
Even hands-on fallback work runs out around **2039**, when I'd be forty.
do: Stay in **buying** for a few years and get properly good at it.
Take a **part-time logistics course** over three years while still working.
Decide with Tomás whether to **buy a flat** or keep renting.
feel: **Anxious** in a slow way, like a long fuse that's still lit.
S4.quote: I'd rather have a baby at thirty with a job than at thirty-six without one.
fieldNote: The ten-year warning pulls **family plans** forward rather than delaying them.
She distrusts the **owners' silence** and trusts Priya (the senior buyer) personally.
Even with a decade, she sees her **income at risk**, so the mood stays anxious.

steps.text: Stay in dry-goods buying and build negotiating skill
Enrol in a part-time logistics course over three years
Decide with Tomás whether to buy a flat or keep renting
Plan a first child earlier, while both still have jobs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question, because I don't have the time or the money to switch fast. What would help is the government paying people to retrain while they're still earning, not after they're already on benefits. And a union that covers office staff, not just the warehouse.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who decides. Nobody asked me whether we buy the ordering system, and nobody will. If workers got a say in how it comes in, I'd be a lot less frightened of it.

headlineQuote: Nobody asked me whether we buy the ordering system, and nobody will. If workers got a say in how it comes in, I'd be a lot less frightened of it.
portrait: Elena is a **27-year-old junior buyer** of dry goods at a food-service distributor, living with Tomás, a bus driver.
She is **still learning**, slow on spreadsheets, and measures herself against Priya, the senior buyer.
She sees her day as **desk thinking work** and expects it to shrink in every scenario but AI Plateau.
Her answer to faster change is **hands-on fallback** work like forklifts and driving, plus union action.
Longer warnings let her **plan licences** and even bring forward having a child.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, because she lacks the time and money to switch fast.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** while still earning, and a **union** that covers office staff.
